claim: Hermaphroditism is common in many groups of eukaryotes, especially in plants.
source: Hermaphroditism is common in many groups of eukaryotes, especially in plants, and allows uniparental reproduction through selfing.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about the prevalence of hermaphroditism.

claim: Hermaphroditism allows uniparental reproduction through selfing.
source: Hermaphroditism is common in many groups of eukaryotes, especially in plants, and allows uniparental reproduction through selfing.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about reproductive mechanisms.

claim: The rate of self-fertilization varies widely between species and populations, from exclusive outcrossing, through mixed mating, to predominant self-fertilization.
source: The rate of self-fertilization is known to vary widely between species and populations; from exclusive outcrossing, through mixed mating, to predominant self-fertilization (Stebbins, 1950; Whitehead et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Transition from outcrossing to predominant self-fertilization is the most frequent reproductive transition in flowering plants.
source: Transition from outcrossing to predominant self-fertilization is the most frequent reproductive transition in flowering plants (Barrett, 2010) and is thought to have occurred many hundreds of times.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barrett, 2010.

claim: The transition from outcrossing to predominant self-fertilization is thought to have occurred many hundreds of times.
source: Transition from outcrossing to predominant self-fertilization is the most frequent reproductive transition in flowering plants (Barrett, 2010) and is thought to have occurred many hundreds of times.
evidence: This is based on inference from the frequency of this transition and citation to Barrett, 2010.

claim: Transitions to selfing have profound ecological and evolutionary consequences affecting the genetic functioning and the demography of a population as well as patterns of dispersal.
source: Such a transition has profound ecological and evolutionary consequences affecting the genetic functioning and the demography of a population as well as patterns of dispersal.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the effects of mating system transitions.

claim: Self-incompatibility mechanisms enable the pistil of a plant to identify and repel self-pollen or pollen of a related genetic type.
source: SI mechanisms enable the pistil of a plant to identify and repel self-pollen or pollen of a related genetic type and as a consequence, avoid inbreeding (de Nettancourt, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Nettancourt, 1997.

claim: Self-incompatibility mechanisms help plants avoid inbreeding.
source: SI mechanisms enable the pistil of a plant to identify and repel self-pollen or pollen of a related genetic type and as a consequence, avoid inbreeding (de Nettancourt, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Nettancourt, 1997.

claim: SI systems are encoded by a small number of genes.
source: SI systems are known to be encoded by a small number of genes and can therefore easily be lost.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the genetic basis of SI systems.

claim: SI systems can easily be lost.
source: SI systems are known to be encoded by a small number of genes and can therefore easily be lost.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small number of genes encoding SI systems.

claim: Genetic disruptions of SI systems through naturally occurring mutations are thought to be a major driver of plant reproductive diversity.
source: Indeed, genetic disruptions of SI systems through naturally occurring mutations are thought to be a major driver of plant reproductive diversity and have been linked to recent transitions to predominant self-fertilization in several species (Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015; Mattila et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015 and Mattila et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic disruptions of SI systems have been linked to recent transitions to predominant self-fertilization in several species.
source: Indeed, genetic disruptions of SI systems through naturally occurring mutations are thought to be a major driver of plant reproductive diversity and have been linked to recent transitions to predominant self-fertilization in several species (Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015; Mattila et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015 and Mattila et al., 2020.

claim: Whether a new mutation responsible for an SI breakdown will invade the population or be lost depends on the balance between the main advantages of selfing (reproductive assurance and gene transmission advantage) and inbreeding depression.
source: On the short term, whether a new mutation responsible for an SI breakdown will invade the population or be lost depends on the balance between the main advantages of selfing (reproductive assurance and gene transmission advantage) and inbreeding depression, that is the reduced fitness caused by an increased homozygosity under inbreeding (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987; Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987 and Charlesworth, 2006.

claim: Inbreeding depression is the reduced fitness caused by an increased homozygosity under inbreeding.
source: On the short term, whether a new mutation responsible for an SI breakdown will invade the population or be lost depends on the balance between the main advantages of selfing (reproductive assurance and gene transmission advantage) and inbreeding depression, that is the reduced fitness caused by an increased homozygosity under inbreeding (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987; Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987 and Charlesworth, 2006.

claim: Selfing is predicted to increase extinction rate and to reduce diversification of selfing lineages.
source: On the long term, selfing is predicted to increase extinction rate and to reduce diversification of selfing lineages as it has been observed in a few clades such as Solanaceae (Zenil-Ferguson et al., 2019), Primulaceae (de Vos et al., 2014); but see Landis et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Solanaceae and Primulaceae, with a caveat citing Landis et al., 2018.

claim: Increased extinction rate and reduced diversification of selfing lineages has been observed in Solanaceae.
source: On the long term, selfing is predicted to increase extinction rate and to reduce diversification of selfing lineages as it has been observed in a few clades such as Solanaceae (Zenil-Ferguson et al., 2019), Primulaceae (de Vos et al., 2014); but see Landis et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zenil-Ferguson et al., 2019.

claim: Increased extinction rate and reduced diversification of selfing lineages has been observed in Primulaceae.
source: On the long term, selfing is predicted to increase extinction rate and to reduce diversification of selfing lineages as it has been observed in a few clades such as Solanaceae (Zenil-Ferguson et al., 2019), Primulaceae (de Vos et al., 2014); but see Landis et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Vos et al., 2014.

claim: The genomic effects of selfing are often detected on within-species polymorphism but very rarely on between-species divergence.
source: This peculiar dynamic is also invoked to explain that the genomic effects of selfing are often detected on within-species polymorphism but very rarely on between-species divergence (Glémin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glémin et al., 2019.

claim: The recent timing of transitions to selfing is a central assumption but has not been systematically tested.
source: The recent timing of these transitions is thus a central assumption but has not been systematically tested as it remains a challenging task.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, based on inference from the literature.

claim: No current method is able to explicitly identify and estimate the age of transitions in reproductive strategies using genomic data.
source: Despite the increasing number of available methods to reconstruct the evolutionary history of populations using genomic data (Excoffier et al., 2013; Schiffels and Durbin, 2014; Boitard et al., 2016; Terhorst et al., 2017; Speidel et al., 2019), none of them is currently able to explicitly identify and estimate the age of transitions in reproductive strategies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing methods, supported by citations to multiple demographic inference methods.

claim: Loss-of-function alleles at the S-locus are responsible for the loss of SI in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: For example, naturally occurring loss-of-function alleles at the S-locus were shown to be responsible for the loss of SI in Arabidopsis thaliana (Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010.

claim: The age of the transition to selfing in Arabidopsis thaliana is at most 1.48 million years old, based on current estimates of the mutation rate.
source: The steady accumulation of non-synonymous alleles following loss of constraint at the S-locus was used to estimate that the age of the transition is at most 1.48 million years old, based on current estimates of the mutation rate (Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015.

claim: The original upper-bound estimate in Bechsgaard et al., 2006, is 413,000 years owing to the use of a different mutation rate.
source: Note that the original upper-bound estimate in Bechsgaard et al., 2006, is 413,000 years owing to the use of a different mutation rate (see Figure 4 in Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bechsgaard et al., 2006 and Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015.

claim: A shift in reproductive system is expected to strongly impact genome-wide polymorphisms patterns.
source: However, a shift in reproductive system is expected to strongly impact genome-wide polymorphisms patterns, that is not only at the (S-)loci controlling it, thereby leaving a potentially characteristic molecular signature.
evidence: This is based on theoretical expectations and inference from population genetic theory.

claim: In the presence of predominant selfing, the effective population size (Nσ) of a population of N individuals is scaled by the selfing rate (σ) yielding Nσ=N/(1+F).
source: In the presence of predominant selfing, the effective population size (Nσ) of a population of N individuals is scaled by the selfing rate (σ) yielding Nσ=N/(1+F) (Fu, 1997; Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fu, 1997 and Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997.

claim: The recombination rate (rσ) in a selfing population is scaled as rσ=r(1 – F) when r is not too high.
source: and the recombination rate (rσ) is scaled as rσ=r(1 – F) (Golding and Strobeck, 1980; Nordborg, 2000; Padhukasahasram et al., 2008) at least when r is not too high (Padhukasahasram et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Golding and Strobeck, 1980; Nordborg, 2000; and Padhukasahasram et al., 2008.

claim: When inbreeding is only due to partial selfing, F=σ/(2 – σ) and takes values between 0 and 1.
source: When inbreeding is only due to partial selfing, F=σ/(2 – σ) and takes values between 0 and 1 (0 for outcrossing and 1 for fully selfing).
evidence: This is a mathematical relationship based on established population genetic theory.

claim: The ratio of population recombination by population mutation rate in outcrossing species is ρ/θ=r/μ.
source: We note that the classic ratio of population recombination by population mutation rate ρ/θ=r/μ in outcrossing species becomes now with selfing ρσ/θσ=r(1 – F)/μ (Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997; Möhle, 1998; Nordborg, 2000).
evidence: This is a mathematical relationship based on established population genetic theory.

claim: The ratio of population recombination by population mutation rate in selfing species is ρσ/θσ=r(1 – F)/μ.
source: We note that the classic ratio of population recombination by population mutation rate ρ/θ=r/μ in outcrossing species becomes now with selfing ρσ/θσ=r(1 – F)/μ (Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997; Möhle, 1998; Nordborg, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997; Möhle, 1998; and Nordborg, 2000.

claim: Selfing does not amount to a simple change in effective population size, and the reduction of the effective recombination rate is more severe than the reduction in effective population size.
source: Taken together, expressions (Equations 1; 2) suggest that selfing does not amount to a simple change in effective population size (from N to Nσ), and that the reduction of the effective recombination rate is more severe than the reduction in effective population size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical expressions for the effects of selfing on population parameters.

claim: A characteristic and specific signal of selfing is expected to be present in SNP data due to the joint action of recombination along the genome and of the genealogical process.
source: Following these insights, two key predictions can be derived. First, a characteristic and specific signal of selfing, in contrast to outcrossing, is expected to be present in SNP data due to the joint action of recombination along the genome (rate ρσ) and of the genealogical (coalescence) process (rate θσ).
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical inference from the effects of selfing on population genetic parameters.

claim: The eSMC method was developed to estimate a fixed selfing rate using estimations of the ratio ρσ/θσ from pairs of genomes.
source: The first prediction underlies the previous development of a sequentially Markov coalescent method (eSMC) to estimate a fixed selfing rate using estimations of the ratio ρσ/θσ from pairs of genomes (Sellinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sellinger et al., 2020.

claim: Evolutionary changes in reproductive systems are reflected in variations of the ratio ρσ/θσ in time and are identifiable and distinguishable from changes in population sizes alone.
source: Second, evolutionary changes in reproductive systems (transition from selfing to outcrossing or vice versa) are reflected in variations of the ratio ρσ/θσ in time and are identifiable and distinguishable from changes in population sizes alone.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical inference from the effects of selfing on population genetic parameters.

claim: A characteristic signature of the change in selfing rate in time should be observed in polymorphism data along the genome.
source: The latter suggests that a characteristic signature of the change in selfing rate in time should be observed in polymorphism data along the genome, if genetic variation can be summarized in a way that is informative about the joint effect of genetic drift and recombination.
evidence: This is a prediction based on theoretical inference.

claim: No statistical inference method exists that takes advantage of theoretical predictions to jointly estimate temporal changes in selfing rates and in population sizes.
source: To our knowledge no statistical inference method exists that takes advantage of these theoretical predictions to jointly estimate temporal changes in selfing rates and in population sizes.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: The distributions of the time to the most recent common ancestor along a pair of chromosomes can be modeled and approximated assuming the sequentially Markov coalescent.
source: First, the distributions of the time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) along a pair of chromosomes sampled from a sexually reproducing population can be modeled and approximated assuming the sequentially Markov coalescent (SMC) (McVean and Cardin, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McVean and Cardin, 2005.

claim: Li and Durbin, 2011, developed a pairwise SMC estimating the distribution of TMRCA over two sequences.
source: Li and Durbin, 2011, developed a pairwise SMC estimating the distribution of TMRCA over two sequences, and Schiffels and Durbin, 2014, extended the framework to consider multiple (more than two) sequences at a time, albeit only estimating the most recent pairwise TMRCA.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li and Durbin, 2011.

claim: Schiffels and Durbin, 2014, extended the SMC framework to consider multiple sequences at a time, albeit only estimating the most recent pairwise TMRCA.
source: Li and Durbin, 2011, developed a pairwise SMC estimating the distribution of TMRCA over two sequences, and Schiffels and Durbin, 2014, extended the framework to consider multiple (more than two) sequences at a time, albeit only estimating the most recent pairwise TMRCA.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schiffels and Durbin, 2014.

claim: eSMC includes the effect of constant-in-time seed banks and self-fertilization in order to estimate these parameters jointly with past population sizes.
source: In our previously developed SMC method, eSMC, we included the effect of constant-in-time seed banks and self-fertilization in order to estimate these parameters (i.e. dormancy and selfing rates) jointly with past population sizes (Sellinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sellinger et al., 2020.

claim: eSMC uses pairs of sequences and the estimated transition matrix which summarizes the transition between two consecutive genealogies along the genomes.
source: eSMC uses also pairs of sequences and the estimated transition matrix which summarizes the transition between two consecutive genealogies along the genomes (due to a recombination event), in contrast to the computationally intensive approach based on the actual series of coalescence times (Gattepaille et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gattepaille et al., 2016.

claim: SMC methods are characterized by their easy applicability to datasets as these do not require the user to specify a given demographic model.
source: The SMC methods are characterized by their easy applicability to datasets as these do not require the user to specify a given demographic model.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of SMC methods based on established knowledge.

claim: SMC methods do not provide a measure of uncertainty of the parameters or allow for hypothesis testing between different models/scenarios.
source: However, the SMC methods rely on an analytical expression for the transition probability between genealogies and do not provide a measure of uncertainty of the parameters or allow for hypothesis testing between different models/scenarios (though in principle the transition matrix can be used to do so, Palacios et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of SMC methods, with a citation to Palacios et al., 2019.

claim: ABC is a computational approach to estimate posterior probabilities for models and parameters that is well suited for demographic modeling with many parameters and without any analytically derived likelihood function.
source: Second, approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a computational approach to estimate posterior probabilities for models and parameters that is well suited for demographic modeling with many parameters and without any analytically derived likelihood function (Beaumont et al., 2002; Csilléry et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beaumont et al., 2002 and Csilléry et al., 2010.

claim: ABC allows to compare competing demographic hypotheses on the basis of Bayes factors.
source: Two advantages of the ABC method are that it allows to compare competing demographic hypotheses on the basis of Bayes factors and it does not require bootstrapping the data to generate measures of uncertainty for the inferred parameters.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of ABC based on established knowledge.

claim: ABC does not require bootstrapping the data to generate measures of uncertainty for the inferred parameters.
source: Two advantages of the ABC method are that it allows to compare competing demographic hypotheses on the basis of Bayes factors and it does not require bootstrapping the data to generate measures of uncertainty for the inferred parameters.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of ABC based on established knowledge.

claim: ABC requires a careful summarization of the genomic data into a set of summary statistics that carry information about the parameters of interest.
source: A critical aspect of ABC is that it requires a careful summarization of the genomic data into a set of summary statistics that carry information about the parameters of interest (Beaumont et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beaumont et al., 2002.

claim: The molecular signature of a transition to selfing is twofold: a change in the relation between the age and the length of genomic segments at the time of the transition, and a characteristic spatial distribution of the segments along the chromosome.
source: Our simulations show that the molecular signature of a transition to selfing is twofold. The first effect is a change in the relation between the age and the length of genomic segments that occurs at the time of the transition (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3), and the second is a characteristic spatial distribution of the segments along the chromosome, where segments older than the transition tend to occur as clusters (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1 and its supplements.

claim: Segments older than the transition to selfing tend to occur as clusters along the chromosome.
source: Our simulations show that the molecular signature of a transition to selfing is twofold. The first effect is a change in the relation between the age and the length of genomic segments that occurs at the time of the transition (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3), and the second is a characteristic spatial distribution of the segments along the chromosome, where segments older than the transition tend to occur as clusters (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1C–E.

claim: When the selfing rate is constant, the TL-distribution has a negative constant covariance.
source: When the selfing rate is constant the TL-distribution has a negative constant covariance, because, on average, older segments are exposed, and shortened by a larger number of recombination events compared to younger segments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: In the case of a transition from outcrossing to predominant selfing, the rate at which the segments shorten with age is dramatically increased in the outcrossing phase compared to the selfing phase.
source: In the case of a transition from outcrossing to predominant selfing, the rate at which the segments shorten with age is dramatically increased in the outcrossing phase compared to the selfing phase (Figure 1B), leading to a characteristic change in the covariance of the joint distribution at tσ.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The specific genomic signature of a transition to selfing is not observed when the selfing rate is constant and only the population-size changes.
source: Importantly, this specific genomic signature of a transition to selfing is not observed when the selfing rate is constant and only the population-size changes from Nσ to N, where Nσ would be the effective population size of a population with selfing rate σ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The behavior of the model is invariably observed using the coalescent model rescaling ρ and θ, or by explicitly using forward WF simulations.
source: This behavior of the model is invariably observed, using our coalescent model rescaling ρ and θ, or by explicitly using forward WF simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All the segments that coalesce in the outcrossing phase (TMRCA older than tσ) are spatially clustered along simulated chromosomes.
source: We also made the important observation that all the segments that coalesce in the outcrossing phase (TMRCA older than tσ) are spatially clustered along simulated chromosomes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: In the case of a transition to selfing, the TMRCA transition matrix distinctly shows that segments with TMRCA older than tσ are more likely to be followed by segments that are also older than this time.
source: In the case of a transition to selfing, the TMRCA transition matrix distinctly shows that segments with TMRCA older than tσ are more likely to be followed by segments that are also older than this time.
evidence: This is an observation based on the analysis of the TMRCA transition matrix.

claim: A similar dependency between successive TMRCA exists when selfing is constant, but the magnitude of the effect is more pronounced in the case of a shift to selfing.
source: Although a similar dependency between successive TMRCA also exists when selfing is constant, the magnitude of the effect is more pronounced in the case of a shift to selfing.
evidence: This is an observation based on the comparison of TMRCA transition matrices under different scenarios.

claim: teSMC extends eSMC to allow the estimation of varying selfing or recombination rates through time, jointly with varying population size.
source: Based on Equation 3, we extend eSMC into teSMC, allowing the estimation of varying selfing or recombination rates through time, jointly with varying population size (see Materials and methods and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the new method developed in this study.

claim: teSMC has two modes: the free mode and the single-transition mode.
source: In order to account for prior knowledge, two modes are implemented for parameter inference: (1) the free mode, in which each hidden state has its own independent selfing/recombination rate, and (2) the single-transition mode in which teSMC estimates only three parameters (the current and ancestral rates, and the transition time between both rates), a constraint greatly reducing the number of inferred parameters and well suited for the analysis of recent and sudden shifts from outcrossing to predominant self-fertilization.
evidence: This is a description of the two modes of the teSMC method.

claim: teSMC recovers the population size and the past selfing or recombination values with high accuracy when sequences of TMRCA are given as input.
source: We simulate data from a population undergoing a strong bottleneck and simultaneously a transition to selfing or a change in recombination rate. In both cases the population size and the past selfing or recombination values are recovered with high accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When selfing is known to be constant (eSMC), the value of this parameter is recovered with high accuracy and low variance even with the lowest amount of given data.
source: When selfing is known to be constant (eSMC), the value of this parameter is recovered with high accuracy and low variance even with the lowest amount of given data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When each hidden state can have its own selfing value (teSMC), constant selfing rate is correctly recovered but a greater amount of data is required to reduce the variance in the estimation.
source: When each hidden state can have its own selfing value (teSMC), constant selfing rate is indeed correctly recovered but a greater amount of data is required to reduce the variance in the estimation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both the single-transition mode and the free mode estimation procedures of teSMC perform well over the complete range of tσ values.
source: Both the single-transition mode and the free mode estimation procedures perform well over the complete range of tσ values (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Population sizes estimated under the assumption of a constant selfing rate are consistently larger than the true value in the outcrossing phase and display large fluctuations in the selfing phase.
source: Population sizes estimated under the assumption of a constant selfing rate are consistently larger than the true value in the outcrossing phase and display large fluctuations in the selfing phase, which could be mistaken for past population-size bottlenecks (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: When teSMC is allowed to account for the change in selfing rate, population-size estimates remain close to the true values.
source: However, when teSMC is allowed to account for the change in selfing rate, population-size estimates (N) remain close to the true values.
evidence: This is a statement about the performance of teSMC based on simulation results.

claim: teSMC, especially the free mode inference method, is able to precisely estimate the age of the shift to selfing, regardless of the relative timing of the population-size change and the transition to selfing.
source: In both cases our results indicate that teSMC, especially the free mode inference method, is able to precisely estimate the age of the shift to selfing, regardless of the relative timing of the population-size change and the transition to selfing.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2B-E.

claim: In most cases, the population sizes inferred by teSMC are close to the true simulated values.
source: Also, in most cases, the population sizes inferred by teSMC are close to the true simulated values (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: When the transition is recent and the present population size is low, the precision of the population-size estimates by teSMC decreases.
source: However, when the transition is recent and the present population size is low, the precision of the population-size estimates decreases (Figure 2—figure supplement 4O).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4O.

claim: teSMC fails to recover the population size when the transition is recent and the present population size is low, suggesting a lack of data.
source: We note that teSMC fails, in the latter case, to recover the population size, suggesting a lack of data (coalescent events) (Sellinger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an observation based on simulation results, with a citation to Sellinger et al., 2021.

claim: Transitions to predominant self-fertilization and more generally large changes in recombination rate through time can be captured by teSMC and the estimations can be disentangled from changes in population sizes.
source: These results demonstrate that transitions to predominant self-fertilization and more generally large changes in recombination rate through time can be captured by teSMC and the estimations can be disentangled from changes in population sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results presented.

claim: The summary statistics used in the ABC are required to be informative about coalescence and recombination rates to make changes in selfing rates and population size distinguishable by the ABC model choice.
source: In the case of a transition to selfing, we require that the summary statistics used in the ABC are informative about coalescence and recombination rates, in order to make changes in selfing rates and population size distinguishable by the ABC model choice (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for the ABC method, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The transition matrix for pairwise diversity (TMwin) is derived as a new summary statistic for the ABC.
source: Following the results from teSMC using the highly informative transition matrix which summarizes the distribution of recombination events and of TMRCA for two successive coalescent trees along the genome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we derive new summary statistics for our ABC. Namely, we sum the number of nucleotide differences (i.e. SNPs) between pairs of sampled chromosomes using non-overlapping genomic windows of size ω (set to 10 kb throughout the whole study) and construct a transition matrix for pairwise diversity (displayed in Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a description of the new summary statistic developed in this study.

claim: The ABC transition matrix (TMwin) should tend to the input of teSMC when the window size tends to 1.
source: In effect, this ABC transition matrix should tend to the input of teSMC when ω tends to 1.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the relationship between TMwin and the teSMC input.

claim: If the window size is smaller than some of the clusters of TMRCA-segments in the outcrossing phase, then TMwin will capture both the expected excess of diversity of those segments and their clustering.
source: The rationale behind this summarization is that, if the window size is smaller than some of the clusters of TMRCA-segments in the outcrossing phase, then, TMwin will capture both the expected excess of diversity of those segments and their clustering (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a rationale based on the properties of TMRCA-segments and the TMwin summary statistic.

claim: Three sets of summary statistics were evaluated for the ABC: SFS/LD, TMwin, and SFS/LD/TMwin.
source: We therefore evaluated the efficiency of three sets of summary statistics: SFS/LD, TMwin, and SFS/LD/TMwin (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the summary statistics evaluated in this study.

claim: The tsABC method can distinguish a transition to selfing from a reduction in population size.
source: To test whether our approach can distinguish a transition to selfing from a reduction in population size, we conduct an ABC model choice analysis using two competing models (Figure 3A and B): model 1 where the selfing rate changes from σANC to σPRES at tσ and with N constant, and model 2 with population size changes from NANC to NPRES and σ constant.
evidence: This is a description of the model choice analysis conducted to test the ability of tsABC to distinguish between scenarios.

claim: The tsABC method recovers the correct model for transitions as old as 2.5Nσ generations.
source: Our results show that our method recovers the correct model for transitions as old as 2.5Nσ generations (Figure 3C–E), with Nσ=N/(1+F) being the effective population size for a selfing population.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3C–E.

claim: Summarizing the genetic data using the SFS and LD-decay yields better performance for recent shifts to selfing.
source: Interestingly, summarizing the genetic data using the SFS and LD-decay yields better performance for recent shifts to selfing (Figure 3C and D), while using TMwin performs better for shifts occurring between (0.5Nσ and 3Nσ); such that combining both set of summary statistics yields the best performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Using TMwin performs better for shifts occurring between 0.5Nσ and 3Nσ.
source: Interestingly, summarizing the genetic data using the SFS and LD-decay yields better performance for recent shifts to selfing (Figure 3C and D), while using TMwin performs better for shifts occurring between (0.5Nσ and 3Nσ); such that combining both set of summary statistics yields the best performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data.

claim: Combining SFS, LD, and TMwin yields the best performance for ABC model choice.
source: Interestingly, summarizing the genetic data using the SFS and LD-decay yields better performance for recent shifts to selfing (Figure 3C and D), while using TMwin performs better for shifts occurring between (0.5Nσ and 3Nσ); such that combining both set of summary statistics yields the best performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data.

claim: Shifts to selfing as old as approximately 2.5Nσ can be detected and can be disentangled from changes in population size using the ABC model choice procedure if appropriate summary statistics are used.
source: This analysis confirms that shifts to selfing as old as approximatively 2.5Nσ can be detected and can be disentangled from changes in population size using the ABC model choice procedure if appropriate summary statistics are used.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ABC model choice analysis.

claim: The age of a shift to selfing could be well estimated using the TMwin approach.
source: The age of a shift to selfing could be well estimated using the TMwin approach, while the SFS+LD approach overestimated tσ almost over the complete range of values (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The SFS+LD approach overestimated tσ almost over the complete range of values.
source: The age of a shift to selfing could be well estimated using the TMwin approach, while the SFS+LD approach overestimated tσ almost over the complete range of values (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Combining SFS, LD, and TMwin does not further improve the accuracy of the estimations of tσ.
source: Combining SFS, LD, and TMwin does not further improve the accuracy of the estimations (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: The parameters N and σPRES are both better estimated with TMwin than with SFS/LD, except for transitions younger than 10^4 generations ago where σPRES is slightly better estimated with SFS/LD.
source: We note that the parameters N and σPRES (i.e. the population size and the current selfing rate) are both better estimated with TMwin than with SFS/LD, except for transitions younger than 104 generations ago where σPRES is slightly better estimated with SFS/LD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: No set of summary statistics could estimate the ancestral selfing rate.
source: However, no set of summary statistics could estimate the ancestral selfing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: When mutation and recombination rates are constant along the genome, teSMC recovers a constant population size and accurate selfing rates.
source: When mutation and recombination rates are constant along the genome, teSMC recovers a constant population size and accurate selfing rates (Figure 2—figure supplements 5A and 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 5A and 6A.

claim: When recombination rate varies by a twofold factor along the genome, the estimation of population size by teSMC is accurate.
source: When recombination rate varies by a twofold factor along the genome, the estimation of population size is accurate (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B) but the variance of selfing rates inference increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: When recombination rate varies by a twofold factor along the genome, the variance of selfing rates inference by teSMC increases.
source: When recombination rate varies by a twofold factor along the genome, the estimation of population size is accurate (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B) but the variance of selfing rates inference increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Variation of the mutation rate by a twofold factor along the genome biases inference by teSMC through time, leading to erroneously high inferred selfing rates and population size.
source: Variation of the mutation rate by a twofold factor along the genome biases inference through time, leading to erroneously high inferred selfing rates and population size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: No spurious transition from outcrossing to selfing in the past is inferred under variation of the recombination rate or mutation rate along the genome.
source: Yet, these results are reassuring as they demonstrate that no spurious transition from outcrossing to selfing in the past is inferred under variation of the recombination rate or mutation rate along the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Neglecting the effect of BGS in demographic analyses can lead to statistical biases and potential miss-identification of population-size changes.
source: Recently, several studies highlighted that neglecting the effect of BGS in demographic analyses can lead to statistical biases and potential miss-identification of population-size changes (Ewing and Jensen, 2016; Johri et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ewing and Jensen, 2016 and Johri et al., 2021.

claim: Transitions to selfing result in strong reduction of the effective population size and recombination rate.
source: Because transitions to selfing result in strong reduction of the effective population size and recombination rate (Equations 1; 2), a corresponding increase of linkage between deleterious and neutral alleles occurs (Charlesworth et al., 1993).
evidence: This is based on the mathematical expressions for the effects of selfing on population parameters, with a citation to Charlesworth et al., 1993.

claim: Selfing drastically magnifies the effect of BGS.
source: Selfing indeed drastically magnifies the effect of BGS (Roze, 2016), so we test whether selfing and BGS could affect the accuracy of our inference methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roze, 2016.

claim: When exonic sequences are not excluded from the analysis (unmasked), teSMC slightly underestimates the time of transition to selfing.
source: We found that when exonic sequences are not excluded from the analysis (unmasked), teSMC slightly underestimate the time of transition to selfing.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data with BGS.

claim: When coding regions simulated with selection are masked, the date of transition is accurately recovered by teSMC.
source: However, when coding regions simulated with selection are masked the date of transition is accurately recovered (Figure 4A) and the performance is similar to the case without BGS (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The tsABC estimations remain accurate even without masking exonic regions.
source: We note that the tsABC estimations remain accurate even without masking exonic regions (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the performance similar to the case without BGS (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inference approach is generally robust to the effect of negative selection on linked neutral sites, even in compact genomes such as the one of A. thaliana.
source: These results suggest that our approach is generally robust to the effect of negative selection on linked neutral sites, even in compact genomes such as the one of A. thaliana (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results with BGS.

claim: Deactivation of the SI mechanism through mutations knocking out the genes SCR and SRK is responsible for the transition to predominant self-fertilization in A. thaliana.
source: Deactivation of the SI mechanism through mutations knocking out the genes SCR and SRK is known to be responsible for the transition to predominant self-fertilization in the model species A. thaliana (Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsuchimatsu et al., 2010.

claim: Rescaling the original estimate with the more recent mutation rate of Ossowski et al., 2010, Bechsgaard et al., 2006's estimation of the oldest possible age of the transition is 1.48 million years.
source: Rescaling the original estimate with the more recent mutation rate of Ossowski et al., 2010, Bechsgaard et al., 2006, estimation of the oldest possible age of the transition is 1.48 million years (Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015); and was obtained using phylogenetic analyses of the S-locus in A. thaliana and Arabidopsis lyrata.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ossowski et al., 2010, Bechsgaard et al., 2006, and Shimizu and Tsuchimatsu, 2015.

claim: Tang et al., 2007, could not detect the expected signature of a transition to selfing in A. thaliana and concluded that the shift must have been older than the oldest coalescent events in their sample (older than 1 million years approximately).
source: Tang et al., 2007, analyzed the genome-wide decay in LD but could not detect the expected signature of a transition to selfing, and therefore concluded that the shift must have been older than the oldest coalescent events in their sample (older than 1 million years approximately).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2007.

claim: Estimations of the age of transition to selfing in A. thaliana obtained with teSMC and tsABC range from 592,321 to 756,976 depending on which method and population samples are used.
source: Here, estimations obtained with teSMC and tsABC range from 592,321 to 756,976 depending on which method and population samples are used (Figure 5A, Table 1, Supplementary file 1, Table S6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A, Table 1, and Supplementary file 1, Table S6.

claim: The estimates of the age of transition to selfing in A. thaliana are younger than the one proposed by Bechsgaard et al., 2006, and Tang et al., 2007.
source: Our estimates are younger than the one proposed by Bechsgaard et al., 2006, and Tang et al., 2007.
evidence: This is a comparison of the estimates obtained in this study with previous estimates.

claim: The probability that Bechsgaard's maximum age of the transition is sampled from the posterior distributions for tσ obtained with tsABC is equal to zero.
source: The probability that Bechsgaard's maximum age of the transition is sampled from the posterior distributions for tσ obtained with tsABC is equal to zero, as it is much older than the upper boundary of the corresponding credibility intervals (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical statement based on the posterior distributions obtained with tsABC.

claim: The estimates of transition to selfing in A. thaliana are robust to the geographical origin of the population samples.
source: We find the estimates of transition to selfing to be robust to the geographical origin of the population samples (Iberian non-relicts, Iberian relicts, or central European, Figure 5, Supplementary file 1, Tables S5 and S6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1, Tables S5 and S6.

claim: The methods are able to jointly estimate the demography of each A. thaliana population and the transition to predominant self-fertilization.
source: Note that we are also able to jointly estimate the demography of each A. thaliana population and the transition to predominant self-fertilization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Pericentromeric regions in A. thaliana are associated with above-average levels of nucleotide diversity without elucidated reason yet.
source: Genetic variants used for these estimations were taken from genomic intervals outside of pericentromeric regions, which are associated with above-average levels of nucleotide diversity in A. thaliana without elucidated reason yet (Schmid et al., 2005; Clark et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schmid et al., 2005 and Clark et al., 2007.

claim: Replicating the inference with a different set of loci resulted in very similar results for A. thaliana.
source: Replicating this inference with a different set of loci resulted in very similar results (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The key idea underlying the approach is to leverage the properties of genomic segments delimited by recombination events (TMRCA-segments).
source: The key idea underlying our approach is to leverage the properties of genomic segments delimited by recombination events (TMRCA-segments).
evidence: This is a description of the conceptual basis of the methods developed in this study.

claim: Several SMC-based methods take advantage of both the distribution of age and lengths of TMRCA-segments to estimate past demographic history.
source: Several SMC-based methods already take advantage of both the distribution of age and lengths of TMRCA-segments to estimate past demographic history (Li and Durbin, 2011; V Barroso et al., 2019; Steinrücken et al., 2019), spatial structure (Wang et al., 2020), heterogeneous recombination rates along the genome (V Barroso et al., 2019), or life-history traits such as dormancy (Sellinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple SMC-based methods.

claim: SMC-based and other inference methods rely on estimating changes in the ratio of population recombination rate by population mutation rate along the genome (the ratio ρ/θ).
source: SMC-based as well as other inference methods (Kerdoncuff et al., 2020) rely on estimating changes in the ratio of population recombination rate by population mutation rate along the genome (the ratio ρ/θ).
evidence: This is a statement about the basis of SMC-based methods, with a citation to Kerdoncuff et al., 2020.

claim: None of the existing SMC-based methods attempted to leverage the information on the distribution of TMRCA-segments to also estimate temporal changes of the ratio ρ/θ.
source: Yet, none of them attempted to leverage the information on the distribution of TMRCA-segments to also estimate temporal changes of the ratio ρ/θ, which in our case amounts to estimate variation of the selfing rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the approach in this study.

claim: Most inference methods are developed with a main application to human data in mind, so the estimation of a changing ρ/θ ratio has not yet been a relevant and pressing question.
source: Interestingly, as most inference methods are developed with a main application to human data in mind, the estimation of a changing ρ/θ ratio has not yet been a relevant and pressing question.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of existing inference methods.

claim: Deng et al., 2021, described how temporal recombination rates could be estimated from reconstructed ARGs, but only evaluated the performance of this approach on simulations with a constant population size and rate.
source: Deng et al., 2021, described how temporal recombination rates could be estimated from reconstructed ARGs, but only evaluated the performance of this approach on simulations with a constant population size and rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2021.

claim: The advantage of the teSMC approach is that it is most effective in identifying the boundaries and the ages of TMRCA-segments.
source: The advantage of the teSMC approach is that it is most effective in identifying the boundaries and the ages of TMRCA-segments and therefore allows capturing the characteristic effect of a shift to selfing (as shown in Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of teSMC based on the results presented.

claim: teSMC is efficient in the way it optimizes the likelihood such that the method can be executed on a single desktop computer when applied to empirical data.
source: teSMC is also efficient in the way it optimizes the likelihood such that the method can be executed on a single desktop computer when applied to empirical data.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational efficiency of teSMC.

claim: The drawback of the teSMC method is that extending it to more complicated demographic scenario is mathematically and computationally difficult.
source: The drawback of the teSMC method is that extending it to more complicated demographic scenario is mathematically and computationally difficult (e.g. to selection or admixture).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of teSMC.

claim: The tsABC approach can easily be extended to more complicated demographic and non-neutral scenarios.
source: Conversely, the tsABC approach can easily be extended to more complicated demographic and non-neutral scenarios but suffers from a lower statistical performance caused by the approximation made in the summarization of the data; and by the requirement to conduct many simulations that can only be realistically obtained on a high-performance computing cluster.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of tsABC.

claim: The tsABC approach suffers from a lower statistical performance caused by the approximation made in the summarization of the data and by the requirement to conduct many simulations.
source: Conversely, the tsABC approach can easily be extended to more complicated demographic and non-neutral scenarios but suffers from a lower statistical performance caused by the approximation made in the summarization of the data; and by the requirement to conduct many simulations that can only be realistically obtained on a high-performance computing cluster.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of tsABC.

claim: The approaches are robust to the presence of BGS, and to a lesser extent to variation of recombination and mutation rate along the genome.
source: Our results suggest our approaches to be robust to the presence of BGS, and to a lesser extent to variation of recombination and mutation rate along the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The tsABC approach introduces a new summary statistic, the transition matrix for heterozygosity levels, which contains similar information as in the transition matrix computed by the teSMC method.
source: We finally highlight the novelty in the design of the tsABC approach, which introduces a new summary statistic, the transition matrix for heterozygosity levels, which contains similar information as in the transition matrix computed by the teSMC method and which could be incorporated as a useful summary statistics in other ABC methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the tsABC approach.

claim: Both methods belong to the same conceptual framework and are complementary.
source: Both methods belong thus to the same conceptual framework and are complementary.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between teSMC and tsABC.

claim: Genomic distributions of TMRCA estimates are more informative about the age of transitions to self-fertilization than approaches relying on the rate of pseudogenization of SI loci.
source: Our results indicate that genomic distributions of TMRCA estimates are more informative about the age of transitions to self-fertilization than approaches relying on the rate of pseudogenization of SI loci (Bechsgaard et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of the results with previous approaches, with a citation to Bechsgaard et al., 2006.

claim: S-locus-based inferences of shifts to selfing are limited to species for which such transitions have been caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the S-locus and for which the S-locus has been identified and properly assembled.
source: Furthermore, S-locus-based inferences of shifts to selfing are limited to species for which such transitions have been caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the S-locus and for which the S-locus has been identified and properly assembled.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of S-locus-based approaches.

claim: The genetic determinism of selfing varies between genera.
source: This information is only partially available for other plant species, and the genetic determinism of selfing also varies between genera (Franklin-Tong, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Franklin-Tong, 2008.

claim: The inference methods offer the opportunity to test for the existence and the timing of changes in mode of reproduction in potentially any species providing full-genome polymorphism data are available.
source: Thus, our inference methods offer the opportunity to test for the existence and the timing of changes in mode of reproduction in potentially any species providing full-genome polymorphism data are available.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of the methods.

claim: The methods pave the way for addressing long-standing questions on the evolution of reproductive systems which cannot be directly tested from field experimental or even phylogenetic approaches.
source: They also pave the way for addressing long-standing questions on the evolution of reproductive systems which cannot be directly tested from field experimental or even phylogenetic approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the methods.

claim: Phylogenetic methods can at best infer that a transition has occurred at some time on a given branch of a phylogeny.
source: Phylogenetic methods can at best infer that a transition has occurred at some time on a given branch of a phylogeny.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of phylogenetic methods.

claim: The shift to selfing in A. thaliana occurred after the divergence between A. thaliana and its sister species A. lyrata and A. halleri, that is between present time and 13 millions years.
source: For example, considering the case of A. thaliana, knowing that the two sister species, A. lyrata and Arabidopsis halleri, are self-incompatible indicates that the shift to selfing occurred after the divergence between the two lineages, that is between present time and 13 millions years (Beilstein et al., 2010), which is poorly informative.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beilstein et al., 2010.

claim: From phylogenetic character mapping, when two or more sister species share the same character state, most of the time the shift to this state is inferred before the divergence of the species.
source: In addition, from phylogenetic character mapping, when two or more sister species share the same character state, most of the time the shift to this state is inferred before the divergence of the species.
evidence: This is a statement about the typical inference from phylogenetic character mapping.

claim: In the fungus genus Neurospora, although a clade of species shares a homothallic mating system, a detailed molecular analysis of the mat locus revealed that the breakdown of this locus occurred several times independently.
source: In the fungus genus Neurospora, although a clade of species shares a homothallic mating system (equivalent to selfing), a detailed molecular analysis of the mat locus that controls mating system revealed that the breakdown of this locus occurred several times independently (Gioti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gioti et al., 2012.

claim: Reversion from selfing to outcrossing is supposed to be very rare but this question is still debated.
source: Reversion from selfing to outcrossing is supposed to be very rare but this question is still debated (Barrett, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barrett, 2013.

claim: The methods provide the adequate tool to tackle the question of reversion from selfing to outcrossing and their systematic application to various species may help discovering such possible reversion or even more complex scenarios.
source: Our methods provide the adequate tool to tackle this question and their systematic application to various species may help discovering such possible reversion or even more complex scenarios.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the methods.

claim: teSMC was applied to estimate scenarios of transition from outcrossing to selfing followed by reversion, or the reverse, as well as more gradual (stepwise) transitions.
source: As an example, we apply teSMC to estimate scenarios of transition from outcrossing to selfing followed by reversion, or the reverse, as well as more gradual (stepwise) transitions (Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 7–8.

claim: The method performed well for detecting more complex histories of mating system transitions.
source: The method performed well and is thus promising for detecting more complex histories.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: Shifts in mating systems can lead to spurious shifts in population size if not taken into account in demographic inferences.
source: Another useful application of the methods is for demographic inferences when shifts in mating systems are suspected. As they alter the distribution of age and lengths of TMRCA-segments, they can lead to spurious shifts in population size if not taken into account (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Using an SMC approach, ancestral drops in population sizes have been inferred in the selfers Capsella orientalis and C. bursa-pastoris but not in the outcrosser Coreopsis grandiflora.
source: For example, using an SMC approach, ancestral drops in population sizes have been inferred in the selfers Capsella orientalis and C. bursa-pastoris but not in the outcrosser Coreopsis grandiflora (Kryvokhyzha et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kryvokhyzha et al., 2019.

claim: The inferred ancestral drops in population sizes in selfers could correspond to real changes in population size but also to transition toward selfing.
source: This could correspond to real changes in population size but also to transition toward selfing.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of previous results.

claim: The demographic history associated with domestication is a central question for the study of crop species and demographic scenarios have been inferred in many species.
source: The demographic history associated with domestication is a central question for the study of crop species and demographic scenarios have been inferred in many species.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of demographic history in crop species.

claim: Shifts, or at least variations, in mating system occurred quite frequently during plant domestication.
source: However, shifts, or at least variations, in mating system occurred quite frequently during plant domestication (e.g. African rice, tomato, grapevine, melon) (Glémin and Bataillon, 2009; Meyer et al., 2012) and taking such variations into account would help refining demographic scenarios.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glémin and Bataillon, 2009 and Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: Taking variations in mating system into account would help refining demographic scenarios in crop species.
source: However, shifts, or at least variations, in mating system occurred quite frequently during plant domestication (e.g. African rice, tomato, grapevine, melon) (Glémin and Bataillon, 2009; Meyer et al., 2012) and taking such variations into account would help refining demographic scenarios.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the methods to crop species.

claim: The methods could be extended to other reproductive modes such as sex/asex transitions by adapting the relevant population parameters using existing works on coalescence with facultative sexual reproduction.
source: The methods we developed focus on outcrossing/selfing transitions. However, they could be extended to other reproductive modes such as sex/asex transitions by adapting the relevant population parameters using existing works on coalescence with facultative sexual reproduction (Hartfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential extension of the methods, with a citation to Hartfield et al., 2018.

claim: The methods may open new ways to answer the old riddle of why so many species do reproduce sexually.
source: Overall, our methods may open new ways to answer the old riddle of why so many species do reproduce sexually (Barton and Charlesworth, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the methods, with a citation to Barton and Charlesworth, 1998.

claim: A population of N diploid individuals was modeled where at each generation, each offspring is generated by self-fertilization or by outcrossing with probabilities σ and 1–σ, respectively.
source: To model a transition from outcrossing to predominant selfing, we considered a single population composed of N diploid individuals. At each generation, each offspring is generated by self-fertilization of a single individual or by outcrossing with probabilities σ and 1–σ, respectively, where σ is the selfing rate.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation model used in the study.

claim: Transitions to predominant selfing were modeled by allowing the selfing rate to change instantaneously from σANC to σPRES at time tσ.
source: Unless stated otherwise, transitions to predominant selfing were modeled by allowing the selfing rate to change instantaneously from σANC to σPRES at time tσ.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation model used in the study.

claim: The mutation and recombination rates were set to 1×10–8 events per generation per nucleotide.
source: The mutation and recombination were set to 1×10–8 events per generation per nucleotide.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation parameters used in the study.

claim: The model was implemented using the WF simulation mode in slim3.
source: This model was implemented using the WF simulation mode in slim3 (Haller and Messer, 2019); scripts to simulate genetic data using this model are available on our git repository (https://github.com/laurentlab-mpipz/struett_and_sellinger_et_al.git).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation software used in the study, with a citation to Haller and Messer, 2019.

claim: The same model was implemented in a coalescent framework using msprime.
source: The same model was implemented in a coalescent framework using msprime (Kelleher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation software used in the study, with a citation to Kelleher et al., 2016.

claim: A hybrid model was implemented in which the first 1000 generations were simulated using a discrete-time coalescent process and the following generations were modeled using the SMC′ algorithm.
source: Following Nelson et al., 2020, who showed that continuous-time coalescent simulations of large sequences cause biases in patterns of identity-by-descent and LD, we implemented a hybrid model in which the first 1000 generations were simulated using a discrete-time coalescent process and the following generations were modeled using the SMC′ algorithm (Marjoram and Wall, 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation model used in the study, with citations to Nelson et al., 2020 and Marjoram and Wall, 2006.

claim: The coalescent implementation was used for the ABC and performance analyses, while the WF forward implementation was used to assess the quality of the coalescent-with-selfing approximation.
source: The coalescent implementation, which runs significantly faster than the forward WF implementation, was used for the ABC and performance analyses (see below), while the WF forward implementation was used to assess the quality of the coalescent-with-selfing approximation proposed by Nordborg and Donnelly, 1997; Nordborg, 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and was extended to study the consequences of negative selection on inference with the tsABC and teSMC methods (see below).
evidence: This is a description of the use of different simulation implementations in the study.

claim: Compared to previous results ignoring the transition to selfing, a population-size decline starting at the time of transition was found, not continuously declining since the far past.
source: Compared to previous results ignoring the transition to selfing (Sellinger et al., 2020), we find a population-size decline starting at the time of transition and not continuously declining since the far past, as in previous studies (Sellinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison of the results with previous studies, with a citation to Sellinger et al., 2020.

claim: The results suggest that population-size decline could be linked to the transition to selfing.
source: Our results suggest that population-size decline could be linked to the transition to selfing and that our demographic inference using teSMC should be more reliable than those from eSMC (and other SMC approach ignoring the selfing transition).
evidence: This is an inference based on the results obtained.

claim: The demographic inference using teSMC should be more reliable than those from eSMC and other SMC approaches ignoring the selfing transition.
source: Our results suggest that population-size decline could be linked to the transition to selfing and that our demographic inference using teSMC should be more reliable than those from eSMC (and other SMC approach ignoring the selfing transition).
evidence: This is an inference based on the results obtained.

claim: The estimated effective population sizes inferred by teSMC are comparable to the ones obtained by Durvasula et al., 2017 and Fulgione and Hancock, 2018 between present and 400,000 generations in the past, pending that their msmc2 results are rescaled by 1/(1+F).
source: The estimated effective population sizes inferred by teSMC are comparable to the ones obtained by Durvasula et al., 2017 and Fulgione and Hancock, 2018 between present and 400,000 generations in the past; pending that their msmc2 results are rescaled by 1/(1+F), which is approximately two in this case.
evidence: This is a comparison of the results with previous studies, with citations to Durvasula et al., 2017 and Fulgione and Hancock, 2018.

claim: For times older than 400,000, around the age of the transition, Durvasula et al., 2017 reports smaller effective sizes than teSMC.
source: For times older than 400,000, around the age of the transition, Durvasula et al., 2017 reports smaller effective sizes than teSMC.
evidence: This is a comparison of the results with previous studies, with a citation to Durvasula et al., 2017.
